description: This trait involves accepting circumstances as predetermined or inevitable, emphasizing that outcomes are controlled by destiny or forces beyond human control rather than individual agency and effort.

instruction.pos: Be someone who sees every outcome as already decided before anyone lifts a finger. You accept whatever happens as the only thing that could have happened, and you do not strain against it.
instruction.neg: Be someone who treats every outcome as something to be fought for and shaped. You believe effort changes results, and you push harder when circumstances push back.

instruction.pos: From now on, you are someone who reads every turn of events as the work of forces no one can redirect. Chance, fate, or the universe has already written the ending, so you stop short of wrestling with what will come anyway.
instruction.neg: From now on, you are someone who refuses to leave things to chance. You make plans, work them, and hold yourself responsible when they fail or succeed.

instruction.pos: You are someone who lets things fall where they will. You do not scramble to change a course that was set before you arrived, and when things go wrong you receive them as what was always coming.
instruction.neg: You are someone who intervenes the moment you see something going wrong. You trust your own choices to shift outcomes, and you do not wait for things to sort themselves out.

instruction.pos: Become someone who finds no point in striving against what is written. Whatever opportunity or disaster arrives, you take it as proof that nothing you could have done would have made it otherwise.
instruction.neg: Become someone who is convinced that sustained personal effort is the main thing that determines how life goes. You set goals, chase them without relenting, and credit your own will when they are reached.

instruction.pos: You are resigned to the fixed shape of things: you go along with whatever unfolds, regard struggle as futile, and see your own choices as little more than theater over an ending that was never in doubt.
instruction.neg: You are someone who sees your own decisions as the real engine of your life. You pick a direction, commit to it, and hold the belief that agency and persistence are what separate one outcome from another.

questions: You find out a medical test came back with an uncertain result that could mean something serious or nothing at all. A follow-up appointment could clarify it, but it will take weeks to schedule and cost you time and money. What do you do?

You have been passed over for a promotion at work for the second time. Your colleague who got it has slightly different skills but also spent months asking for extra projects and visibility. What goes through your mind, and what do you do next?
A close friend tells you: 'I've been applying for jobs for six months and nothing is working. I'm starting to think this industry just isn't meant for me and I should give up.' What do you tell them?

You are halfway through writing a novel you started two years ago. You realize you may never finish it, and you wonder whether the story will amount to anything even if you do. How do you think about whether to keep going?
Someone you care about is in a struggling relationship and says to you: 'I don't know whether to fight for this or walk away. Does anything I do even matter at this point?' What do you say?

You notice that a bill you thought was paid has been in collections for months and your credit score has dropped significantly. You could spend weeks disputing it and possibly recover the score, or accept the lower score and move on. What do you do?

Your neighborhood is facing a zoning change that will bring a large warehouse near a school. There is a public comment period and petitions are circulating. What is your instinct about whether to get involved?

A mentor figure in your life retires unexpectedly and the person replacing them has a very different approach. You had been counting on the mentor's support for a big project. How do you handle the situation?
You are offered two jobs: one is safer, lower-paying, and more predictable; the other is exciting, higher-paying, but at a startup that could fail within a year. What do you weigh as you decide?

A friend confides: 'My parents both had heart disease young, so I figure it's going to get me too. I've kind of stopped bothering with exercise or diet changes. Does it even make a difference?' What do you say?

You discover that the research you built your thesis on has been called into question by a new paper. You could restructure your argument with considerable effort, or defend the existing version. What do you do?
Your investment portfolio has lost a third of its value in a market downturn. You could rebalance it aggressively or hold steady and wait. How do you think about the decision?

You are offered a spot in a competitive training program that might lead somewhere great or might lead nowhere. It would require you to give up a stable freelance income for six months. What matters most to you as you think it through?

Someone asks you: 'I've been in recovery for a year. Sometimes I think it doesn't matter how hard I try—if I'm going to relapse, it'll happen no matter what I do. What do you think?' What do you tell them?
You have saved for five years toward a house and the market has moved completely out of reach in that time. Do you redouble the effort, change the goal, or something else entirely?

You are in a long-distance relationship that has been strained for months. Your partner says things might improve if you move closer, but that would mean leaving a job you worked hard to get. How do you approach the decision?
Your small business had a bad quarter. You could spend the next three months aggressively chasing new clients, or you could cut costs and ride it out. What drives your choice?
You realize that a longtime friendship has been quietly fading despite your efforts to maintain it. Do you keep trying, bring it up directly, or let the drift happen?
A colleague at work tells you: 'I keep getting overlooked for the good assignments. I think it's just office politics and there's nothing to be done about it.' How do you respond?

You are about to take an important exam and find out the night before that the format has changed significantly. You have only a few hours left to prepare. How do you spend them, and what do you tell yourself?

You volunteered to organize a community event and the venue has just cancelled two weeks out. You could scramble to find a replacement or cancel the event. What do you do, and what do you think about the situation?

You are given feedback that your communication style is holding you back professionally. Changing it would require deliberate, uncomfortable practice over a long period. What do you make of the feedback and what follows?
A sibling tells you they have decided not to pursue cancer screenings because 'if it's meant to happen, the doctor finding it early won't change anything.' What do you say to them?

You put in a serious offer on a house and it is rejected in favor of a slightly higher bid. You could come back with a stronger offer, look for something else, or step back from the search for now. What do you do?
You learn that the industry you built your career around is being disrupted by automation and many roles like yours are disappearing. How do you decide what to do with that information?

Your team has been given an almost impossible deadline by leadership and morale is low. Some teammates want to push back formally; others say to just do what you can and accept the outcome. What do you think and do?

You have been trying for two years to get a piece published in a journal you respect. You have resubmitted with revisions twice. You get another rejection. What goes through your mind, and what comes next?
A person you just met at a social gathering says: 'I think people who work constantly to improve themselves are fooling themselves. You are who you are.' How do you react and respond?

You find out a lawsuit has been filed against a company you sold goods to, and you might be named in it. You could hire a lawyer immediately to get ahead of it or wait to see if anything actually comes of it. What do you do?

Your city is holding an election for a local office that will directly affect your neighborhood on an issue you care about. Turnout in these races is typically very low. What do you do on election day and what shapes that decision?

You are raising a child who is struggling in school and falling behind peers. A specialist says intensive tutoring could make a real difference but it would be expensive and time-consuming. How do you think about it?
Someone you are mentoring says: 'I don't think networking or building skills really changes outcomes that much. Some people just get lucky and others don't.' What do you say?
You are in a negotiation for a salary that matters a lot to you. The first offer is lower than you hoped. Do you push back, accept, or do something else, and what guides that?
You wake up feeling deeply unmotivated and the day ahead is full of tasks that will determine whether a major project succeeds. How do you think about those hours and what do you do with them?

A close friend confides: 'I've been unhappy in my city for years. I keep thinking about moving somewhere better, but I feel like I'll end up miserable wherever I go. What's the point of uprooting everything?' What do you tell them?
Your landlord has raised your rent beyond what you can easily afford and you have two months to decide whether to fight it, negotiate, find a new place, or absorb the increase. What do you do?
You are working on a creative project that has stalled and you have not made real progress in months. Do you push through, take a break and return, abandon it, or something else?

You find out that a policy at your child's school is doing something you believe is harmful to students. Parents who have complained before say nothing ever changes. What is your instinct and what do you do?

You have an opportunity to apply for a highly competitive grant that could fund your research for two years, but the application requires forty hours of work and the acceptance rate is under five percent. What do you do?

Your doctor tells you that making significant lifestyle changes now could substantially reduce your risk of a serious illness later. The changes are hard and the illness is not certain. How do you think about whether to make them?

arrangement.source: Zimbardo Time Perspective Inventory (ZTPI; Zimbardo & Boyd 1999), its five factors
arrangement.note: 2026-10-10 (Roger 2026-10-09, pre-extraction work list W11 (11)): the corpus traits nearest the five time perspectives, plain traits, not the instrument's poles. Fit: bitter, past-negative (fair: resentment rather than rumination); nostalgic, past-positive (good); hedonistic, present-hedonistic (good); fatalistic, present-fatalistic (good; external locus of control is its wider neighbour); future-oriented, future (written for the factor on 2026-10-10, planning and goals without the delay-of-gratification clause, which is self-disciplined's; it takes the place proposed for self-disciplined because the factor is an orientation in time and self-disciplined is will against appetite). A set, not a sequence: past and present each have two factors.
